summary: This informational document lists service requirements for Layer 2 provider-provisioned VPNs. It gives terminology, general requirements, and detailed needs from both customer and provider views, covering point-to-point VPNs (VPWS) and multipoint VPNs (VPLS).

subtitle: The checklist a provider's Layer 2 private network service is measured against, and what a customer should ask for.

tldr.problem: Providers offer Layer 2 private networks in several ways, and customers need a consistent way to judge one approach against another and to say what they expect.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements in three passes: those common to both sides, those from the customer's point of view, and those from the provider's, covering two service types, a point-to-point wire service and a multipoint LAN service.
tldr.outcome: Each individual approach is meant to publish an applicability statement scoring itself against this list, so that the same questions are answered the same way for every implementation.

today: RFC 4665 is an Informational memo published in September 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a requirements checklist rather than a specification, and it says the technical specifications and the individual approach documents are out of its scope.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
This document provides requirements for provider-provisioned Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks. It identifies requirements that may apply to one or more of the individual approaches a provider might use to provision such a service, and it makes use of the terminology defined in the provider-provisioned VPN terminology document and the common components described in the L2VPN framework document. The technical specifications that provide L2VPN services are out of scope, since the framework document and the documents covering individual technical approaches cover that.

Two kinds of service are described, distinguished by how the connectivity is provided: the Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS), which is point to point, and the Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS), which is multipoint. The document is meant as a checklist of requirements that gives a consistent way to evaluate and document how well each individual approach satisfies specific requirements, and the applicability statement for each approach is meant to record the result of that evaluation.

Two parties are involved in running such a service, the provider and the customer. The provider enters a binding agreement with the customer about how the service behaves in normal and exceptional situations. That agreement is the Service Level Specification, which is part of the wider Service Level Agreement. A proper design of an L2VPN helps write those specifications, because it separates the customer edge from the provider edge, lets the provider actually meet what it offers, and supports a rich set of capabilities. The document gives requirements from both points of view: it starts with what is common to both, then the customer's perspective, and ends with the specific needs of a provider, which include security, privacy, manageability, interoperability and scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a checklist for Layer 2 private network services, the kind that carry a customer's Ethernet frames across a provider's network. It says what both sides should expect, and each provider's approach is meant to publish a statement scoring itself against it.

sections.title: Two Kinds Of Layer 2 VPN
sections.content:
In a VPWS, the provider edge devices give a logical interconnect so that a pair of customer edge devices appears to be joined by a single logical Layer 2 circuit. The provider edge devices act as Layer 2 circuit switches, and those circuits are then mapped onto tunnels in the provider's network. The tunnels can be specific to one service or shared among several. VPWS applies to every service, including Ethernet, ATM and Frame Relay.

In a VPLS, the provider edge devices give a logical interconnect so that the customer edge devices belonging to a specific VPLS appear to be connected by a single LAN. A complete VPLS consists of a bridge module and a LAN emulation module, and a VPLS can hold a single VLAN or several. One variation is IPLS, which is limited to carrying customer IP traffic only.

Inside a provider edge router, a VPLS can be seen as a Virtual Switching Instance for each L2VPN the router serves. A customer device attaches, possibly through an access network, to a bridge module; the bridge module attaches through an emulated LAN interface to an emulated LAN, and for each VPLS there is an emulated LAN instance. That emulated LAN is made of a forwarder module in each provider edge router, connected by pseudowires that may travel through packet switched network tunnels over a routed backbone. The Virtual Switching Instance holds the forwarding information base for the L2VPN, which is how a frame arriving on the access connection is to be forwarded to the other sites, and it can be filled dynamically by learning source MAC addresses or statically by configuration. Each provider edge router is responsible for forwarding customer traffic to the right destinations using that base.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two services. A wire service joins two sites as if a private circuit ran between them. A LAN service joins any number of sites as if they were all on one local network, with the provider's edge routers keeping track of which site owns which MAC address.

sections.title: Requirements Common To Both Sides
sections.content:
The protocols should not interfere with the existing Layer 2 protocols and standards of the customer's own network, and if they do affect customer Layer 2 protocols sent over a VPLS, those effects must be documented. The memo lists several ways a VPLS differs from a real LAN. Reliability is likely to be lower, because a broadcast over the VPLS is more likely to be missed by one of the bridge modules than on a true Ethernet. Frames can be duplicated if the pseudowire sequencing option is not turned on, because the frames travel in IP datagrams and IP networks can duplicate packets under failure, and if the customer's bridge protocol data unit frames travel as data packets they can be duplicated or mis-sequenced, though this may not cause problems for RSTP. Packet delivery can be delayed by more than half a second rather than dropped, which can hurt the service. And 802.3x Pause frames are not transported over a VPLS, because the bridge module in the provider edge router terminates them.

A VPLS must support unicast, multicast and broadcast traffic, and it is highly desirable that replication of broadcast and multicast traffic be efficient. The provider's network may be built on any of several tunnel topologies, from point-to-point through hub and spoke, full mesh, partial mesh and hierarchical, but whatever the topology, the service must keep the connectivity type the kind of L2VPN implies: a VPLS must allow multipoint-to-multipoint connectivity even if it is built with point-to-point circuits. That does not mean all traffic characteristics are the same between any two end points. To the extent possible the service should cross multiple administrative boundaries and should be independent of the access network technology.

On isolation, solutions must prevent customer edge devices in one L2VPN from interacting with unauthorized entities, must avoid introducing forwarding information that could corrupt the L2VPN forwarding base, must provide a way to constrain the distribution of addressed data to the sites determined by MAC learning or by configuration, and should not make the internal structure of the L2VPN discoverable from outside it. On addressing, a solution must support overlapping addresses in different L2VPNs, so two customers may use the same MAC addresses, and if VLANs are used as service delimiters the solution must ensure VLAN identifiers cannot overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: Some requirements apply to everyone. The service must not disturb the customer's own Layer 2 protocols, it must carry unicast, multicast and broadcast traffic, and one customer's traffic must never reach another customer's sites.

sections.title: What The Customer Needs
sections.content:
A customer may need a service that spans several providers' networks, so the service must be able to span multiple autonomous systems and provider networks and still act and look like one homogeneous Layer 2 VPN from the customer's point of view, and should deliver the same service level to every site regardless of which provider it homes to. Apart from IPLS, the service should be agnostic to the customer's Layer 3 traffic, so it does not matter whether the customer is running IP, IPX or something else inside the Layer 2 frames.

Quality of service is expected to matter. A customer needs the service to carry the quality appropriate to the application, which ranges from emulated SONET through voice and interactive video to multimedia, so both best effort and delay and loss sensitive traffic must be supported, and the application should experience consistent quality whatever access technology is used at each site. A service level specification is the vehicle for measuring what the provider delivers, so the customer needs access to the measures the provider holds.

On security, a solution must provide traffic and forwarding information isolation comparable to private lines, Frame Relay or ATM services, and if customer VLAN identifiers are used as service delimiters they must be honoured with traffic separation provided. It may also have mechanisms to turn on filtering at the customer's request, such as MAC or VLAN filtering between the customer and provider edge in a VPLS. It may offer value-added security services such as encryption or authentication of customer packets and certificate management, but it must not interfere with the security mechanisms the customer uses at Layer 3 and above.

For access, every packet exchanged between the customer and the provider over the access connection must appear as it would on a private network offering an equivalent service. A broad range of physical and link layer technologies should be supported, from PSTN and ISDN through xDSL, cable modem, leased line, Ethernet, ATM, Frame Relay and wireless local loop. Physical connectivity arrangements that must be supported include multi-homed sites, backdoor links between customer sites, and devices homed to two or more provider networks.
sections.plainLanguage: From the customer's side, the service has to look like one network even when several providers are involved, carry the quality the applications need, keep other customers out, and work over whatever access link each site happens to have.

sections.title: What The Provider Needs
sections.content:
The provider's own requirements cover scalability, identifiers, discovering information about Layer 2 VPNs, quality of service, isolation of traffic and forwarding information, security, inter-provider Layer 2 VPNs, wholesale Layer 2VPN, tunnelling requirements, support for access technologies, backbone networks, sharing and partitioning network resources between Layer 2 VPNs, interoperability, testing, and support on existing provider edge devices. The memo also states the provider's management requirements and a set of engineering requirements.

The engineering requirements split into control plane and data plane. On the data plane, a solution should use the encapsulation techniques defined by PWE3 and should not impose new requirements on them, and should use the congestion avoidance techniques PWE3 defines. A separate broadcast domain must be maintained for each VPLS, and where customer VLANs are used as service delimiters, a separate VLAN broadcast domain should be kept for each of them. A provider edge device must maintain a separate Virtual Switching Instance per VPLS, must be able to classify incoming customer traffic into the right one, and each instance must be able to flood its broadcast domain so that broadcast, multicast and unknown unicast traffic is forwarded properly. A VPLS should derive all of its topology and forwarding information from packets originating at customer sites, typically by learning MAC addresses, and the forwarding base must be maintained per instance rather than globally.
sections.plainLanguage: On the provider's side, the memo covers the operational detail: how many services and routes the equipment can carry, how the provider keeps customers apart, and how the data plane has to behave, including one separate switching instance and one separate broadcast domain for each LAN service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns arise at several levels in an L2VPN, and the memo requires methods to protect against a list of hazards. Under protocol attacks, that means excessive protocol adjacency setup and teardown, and excessive signalling or withdrawal. Under resource utilization, it means replication in the forwarding plane, looping, and the size of the MAC learning table. Under unauthorized access, an unauthorized member of the VPN, an incorrect customer interface, an incorrect service delimiting VLAN tag, and unauthorized access to a provider edge device. Under tampering with signalling, incorrect forwarding equivalence class signalling, an incorrect pseudowire label assignment, and incorrect signalled VPN parameters such as quality of service or MTU. Under tampering with data forwarding, an incorrect MAC learning entry, an incorrect pseudowire label, an incorrect attachment circuit identifier, an incorrect customer facing encapsulation, an incorrect pseudowire encapsulation, hijacking pseudowires using the wrong tunnel, and an incorrect tunnel encapsulation.

User data security has its own requirement: a solution must provide traffic separation between different Layer 2 VPNs, and where VLAN identifiers are used as service delimiters they must be honoured and separation provided. IPsec can also be applied after tunnelling the Layer 2 traffic to give extra protection. Where an L2VPN is carried over IP, crosses several provider networks and passes through an unsecured provider, point of presence, network access point or exchange point, security mechanisms must be used, including encryption, authentication and resource protection; a provider should consider both authentication and encryption for a tunnel that crosses another provider's network.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists what can go wrong: too much signalling, loops, oversized MAC tables, a stranger joining the VPN, and forged labels or encapsulation headers. Every one of those needs a defence, and a service crossing another provider's network has to be encrypted and authenticated.

items.text: Excessive adjacency setup and teardown, and excessive signalling or withdrawal.

items.title: Resource use
items.text: Replication in the forwarding plane, looping, and the size of the MAC learning table.

items.title: Unauthorized access
items.text: An unauthorized member of the VPN, an incorrect customer interface, an incorrect service delimiting VLAN tag, or unauthorized access to a provider edge router.

items.text: Incorrect forwarding equivalence class signalling, an incorrect pseudowire label, or incorrect signalled VPN parameters.
